content: A zwitterion is a chemical compound that is electrically neutral overall but contains both a formal positive charge and a formal negative charge on different atoms within the molecule. The term zwitterion is derived from the German word Zwitter, meaning hybrid or hermaphrodite. These compounds are polar in nature and typically exhibit high solubility in water while demonstrating poor solubility in most organic solvents. Ampholytes are molecules that possess both acidic and basic functional groups, making them amphoteric in nature. At a specific pH, known as the molecule's isoelectric point, these ampholytes exist in their zwitterionic form. Ampholytic molecules are particularly effective as buffering agents because they resist changes in the pH of a solution through selective ionization. In acidic environments, they accept hydrogen ions, thereby removing these ions from the solution. Conversely, in basic environments, they donate hydrogen ions to the solution, helping to maintain pH balance. Common examples of zwitterions include compounds used as buffering agents, many of which are part of Good's buffers. These include amino-sulfonic acid-based compounds such as MES (2-(N-morpholino)ethanesulfonic acid), MOPS (3-(N-morpholino)propanesulfonic acid), HEPES (4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid), PIPES (piperazine-N,N′-bis(2-ethanesulfonic acid)), and CAPS (3-(cyclohexylamino)-1-propanesulfonic acid). Additionally, amino-carboxylic acid-based compounds, such as glycine and its derivatives (bicine and tricine), as well as alanine, are also examples of zwitterions. Zwitterions are also utilized as detergents, such as CHAPSO (3-(cholamidopropyl)dimethylammonio-2-hydroxy-1-propane sulfonate). Natural products like the alkaloids psilocybin and lysergic acid also exist in zwitterionic forms. Betaines, another class of zwitterions, are commonly encountered in biological systems. Less common examples of zwitterions include quinonoid zwitterions and certain pharmaceutical drugs, such as fexofenadine (marketed as Allegra®).
